newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Strikes, blockades paralyse much of Bulgaria.
newsitem.headline: Strikes, blockades paralyse much of Bulgaria.

text.p: Opposition supporters paralysed much of Bulgaria with roadblocks and strikes on Monday as protests to demand a general election entered their fifth week.
Sofia students played soccer and volleyball in main street junctions and public transport stopped in Sofia and the second city of Plovdiv.
One man brought a piano out of his central Sofia home into the centre of a boulevard and started serenading passers by.
Many commuters were sympathetic to the disruption. "If walking is what it takes to bring the communists down from power, I'll walk until the end of the year," said a middle-aged housewife in Sofia.

Main international routes were blocked around the country, national radio said. All roads around Plovdiv were closed, a human chain blocked the town of Iambol for two hours, and protesters closed a main bridge in Varna port.
Demonstrators at Doupnitsa, 60 km (35 miles) south of Sofia, kept up their round-the-clock barricade of road and rail routes to Greece for a sixth day.
National police chief Hristo Marinsky appealed to politicians and to President Petar Stoyanov to find a way of keeping the protests peaceful and avoiding violence.
National radio reported strikes at all the country's mines and said Sofia airport would close to incoming flights for an hour from 3 p.m. (1300 GMT).

Protesters from the Kremikovtsi steelworks planned to join demonstrators surrounding the Socialist headquarters, where the party meets later on Monday to discuss a new government, Bulgaria's ninth since the end of communist rule in 1989.
The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) on Sunday declined the Socialists' last-minute offer of more talks on a coalition, saying they must first hand back their mandate.

The state news agency BTA said a six-day blockade of road and rail links between Bulgaria and Greece had prevented more than 1,000 freight wagons carrying food, coal, liquid fuels and medicine from entering the country.
Distribution workers at Neftochim, Bulgaria's largest oil refinery, started one-hour daily stoppages on Thursday.
Several towns have complained of fuel and bread shortages.
Bulgaria's government has been paralysed since December when Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned after months of criticism of his handling of the economy.

While the Balkan state has sunk further into crisis, urgent legislation has been left unattended such as voting the 1997 budget and setting up a tough fixed exchange rate regime to restore confidence in the national currency.
The lev, in freefall since the start of the year, traded at 2,400-2,500 on the interbank market on Monday compared to 1,930-2,000 at Friday's close. It traded at 70 to the dollar a year ago.
Both the European Union and the International Monetary Fund have said that there can be no efforts to help Bulgaria out of crisis until a stable government is in place.

The Socialists have an absolute majority in parliament and barring defections, should be able to win a vote of confidence for their cabinet on Tuesday, but many people fear a repeat of the violence which broke out between police and demonstrators who besieged and ransacked the legislature on January 10.
Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, designated to form a new Socialist government, tried on Friday to propose a compromise way out but failed to win the backing of the party leadership.

In an apparently unrelated development, former military prosecutor General Lilko Yotsov and his wife were badly wounded by a bomb which exploded in their car on Monday. Car bombs are frequently used to settle scores in Bulgaria, where the crime rate has soared since the end of communist rule in 1989.
